Research Proposal: Compositional Reasoning Under Distraction — When Do Agentic
Workflows Break Down?

Title**"Plan-Trace-Verify: A Controlled Study of Multi-Step Compositional
Reasoning in LLM Agents Under Distractor Conditions"**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based agents today are deployed on tasks that require chaining
multiple reasoning steps (e.g., "book a flight, check the weather at the
destination, then find restaurants within budget"). These agents frequently fail
not because individual steps are hard, but because they lose the thread when
intermediate results contradict expectations or when irrelevant context
(distractors) is injected mid-trajectory.

The core problem: existing benchmarks evaluate reasoning in clean, single-turn
settings (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA), but agentic reasoning involves iterative
plan-trace cycles where earlier outputs become inputs to later steps. We lack a
controlled benchmark that isolates the effect of "distractor injection" —
irrelevant or misleading intermediate observations — on compositional reasoning
accuracy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
H₁ (Primary): Injecting task-irrelevant but semantically plausible
observations mid-trajectory degrades LLM agent compositional reasoning accuracy
by ≥25% relative to the no-distractor baseline, even when the underlying
reasoning path is unchanged.

H₂ (Mechanism): The degradation is primarily driven by retrieval interference
(the agent attends to distractor tokens in subsequent reasoning steps) rather
than plan corruption (the agent incorrectly revises its plan). This implies that
improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

H₃ (Mitigation): A simple Plan-Trace-Verify loop — where the agent explicitly
writes down its plan before execution, traces each step against the plan after
receiving observations, and verifies consistency before proceeding — recovers
≥80% of the performance gap relative to the no-distractor baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Framework: Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV)

We define three agent strategies to compare:

1 Direct-ReAct (baseline): Standard ReAct-style agent — thinks, acts, observes
in a flat loop with no explicit plan tracking.
2 Plan-then-Execute (ablation control): The agent writes a plan (as pseudocode
or bullet points) before execution, then follows it linearly, but does not
re-check consistency after each observation.
3 Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV) (proposed): The agent:

• Plan: Writes an explicit, numbered plan with preconditions and expected
postconditions for each step.
• Trace: After each observation, appends a structured trace entry: [Step N]
expected=<...> observed=<...> match=<yes|no>.
• Verify: Before the next step, runs a consistency check. If match=no, the
agent must decide: (a) proceed (the mismatch is benign), (b) re-plan from
this state, or (c) request clarification.

Distractor Injection ProtocolFor each task, we construct three conditions:

• Clean: Standard trajectory, no distractors.
• Weak distractors: One irrelevant observation per task, semantically related
to the domain but logically unnecessary (e.g., a flight search returns "Did
you know? Economy seats have30-inch pitch." between steps).
• Strong distractors: Two to three irrelevant observations, written to
plausibly contradict an intermediate expectation without actually
invalidating the correct path (e.g., a weather lookup returns "Rain expected"
when the correct reasoning only needs temperature).

Distractors are inserted at fixed positions (after step1, after step2) to ensure
controlled comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct CompAgent-Distract, a synthetic multi-step
compositional reasoning dataset with500 tasks spanning three domains:

Domain                    Example Task                 Steps  Distractor Slots
Travel planning           "Book the cheapest flight    4–6    After steps1,3
to a city with population
<1M and good hiking
within50km"
Scientific literature QA  "Find the paper that         3–5    After step2
introduced method X, check
if it was published
before2020, and list its
citations that also use
dataset Y"
Multi-hop tool use        "Get the current time in     4–5    After steps1,2
Tokyo, convert to UTC, find
a meeting slot that works
for a New York participant"

Each task has:

• A gold answer (deterministic)
• A correct reasoning trace (verifiable by exhaustive enumeration)
• One clean + two distractor variants (weak, strong) -3 random seeds for
distractor surface form variationWe also evaluate on AgentQA (a subset of200
multi-turn agent tasks) for out-of-distribution generalization.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary? |

|---|---|---| | Step-level accuracy | Fraction of reasoning steps where the
correct action/observation is selected given the history | Yes | | Final answer
accuracy | Exact-match (or programmatic equivalence) of the final output | Yes |
| Plan deviation rate | Fraction of episodes where the agent's actions diverge
from the optimal plan (measured by trace alignment) | Secondary | | Recovery
rate | Fraction of distractor episodes where the agent corrects itself before
the final step | Secondary | | Token cost overhead | Total input + output tokens
relative to Direct-ReAct | Efficiency |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals (bootstrap, N=1000) across3
seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why |

|---|---|---| | Direct-ReAct | Flat thought-action-observation loop | Standard
minimal agent; lower bound | | Plan-then-Execute | Pre-plan, no mid-trajectory
verification | Isolates the value of verification vs planning | | ReAct +
Self-Consistency | Sample5 trajectories, majority vote final answer | Tests
whether ensembling helps with distractors | | ReAct + Reflexion | Agent
verbalizes feedback after failure | Tests whether post-hoc reflection recovers
from distractors | | GPT-4o / Claude3.5 Sonnet (zero-shot) | No ReAct, just
prompt with tools | Measures intrinsic reasoning without agent scaffolding |

All baselines use the same backend LLM (we control for model; primary
experiments use a frontier model, with a secondary pass on an open-weight model
like Llama-3-70B).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Distractor position: Do distractors hurt more at early vs late
steps?

2 Distractor type: Semantic distractors vs random tokens vs plausible-but-wrong
facts — which causes the most degradation?
3 Plan granularity: Does a detailed plan (per-step pre/post conditions) help
more than a brief plan (bullet list)?
4 Verification frequency: Verify after every step vs every2 steps vs
end-of-trajectory — is there a sweet spot?
5 Memory structure: Instead of PTV's trace-and-verify, use a simple scratchpad
with a "recent observations" summary — does structured memory alone match
PTV?
6 Model scale: Does the gap between PTV and Direct-ReAct shrink or grow at
larger model sizes?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | What to Watch For | Mitigation in Design
|

|---|---|---| | PTV overhead overwhelms small models | PTV may degrade
performance on <7B models because long traces consume context and confuse the
model | Evaluate on ≥7B; report token cost; consider ablation (ablation4:
verification frequency) | | Distractors too weak to cause degradation | If
accuracy stays at90%+, the manipulation check fails | Pilot-test distractor
strength on a development set; reject distractors that cause <5% drop on3 random
runs. If needed, escalate to "adversarial distractors" written to specifically
match common LLM failure patterns | | Plan quality variance swamps the effect |
If some agents write poor plans, plan deviation may correlate with plan quality,
not distractor handling | Pre-validate plan quality: only include episodes where
the initial plan is judged correct by an automated verifier (a separate LLM call
with rubric) | | No gap between Plan-then-Execute and PTV | If verification
doesn't help, hypothesis H₃ is falsified — but H₁ and H₂ remain testable | This
is still informative: it would suggest that planning alone (without per-step
verification) suffices for distractor robustness. We would then investigate
whether the agent implicitly verifies during planning | | Recovery rate near0 |
Agents detect mismatches but do not correct | Distinguish detection vs recovery
in metric design; if detection is high but recovery low, that's a different
(useful) finding about agentic decision-making under uncertainty | | Distractor
position confounds step difficulty | Earlier steps in a task may be
systematically easier/harder | Counterbalance: permute step order for a subset
of tasks and re-run the strongest distractor condition |

# Graph Rewiring: Dynamic Restructuring of Reasoning Graphs for Adaptive AI Agents

Short Hypothesis: Allowing an AI agent to dynamically restructure its reasoning graph (adding, removing, or merging nodes and edges) based on intermediate feedback will significantly improve performance on complex multi-step reasoning tasks, especially those requiring plan revision, compared to static graph-of-thought methods or simple backtracking.

Related Work: Existing reasoning frameworks for LLM agents include Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Tree-of-Thought (ToT), Graph-of-Thought (GoT), and ReAct. CoT uses linear steps with no revision. ToT uses tree search with backtracking but only allows retracing a single path. GoT predefines a static DAG structure and does not allow dynamic modification. ReAct interleaves reasoning and action but lacks structured graph revision. My proposal uniquely introduces dynamic graph rewiring: the agent can insert, delete, or merge nodes and edges during reasoning, enabling non-linear structural adaptation based on new information. This goes beyond simple backtracking by allowing the entire reasoning topology to change.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often struggle with complex reasoning tasks that require revising plans or assumptions after partial execution. Existing methods such as Chain-of-Thought, Tree-of-Thought, and Graph-of-Thought impose fixed reasoning structures (linear, tree, or static DAG) that limit adaptability. We propose Graph Rewiring, a novel framework where the agent maintains a dynamic reasoning graph that it can restructure on the fly. At each step, the agent can expand a node, retract a node (with backtracking), merge two nodes (combining parallel subproblems), or insert a new node between existing nodes (reformulating the reasoning path). These operations are decided by the LLM itself based on the current graph state and intermediate observations. We evaluate on HotpotQA (multi-hop QA) and a custom Dynamic Puzzle benchmark where new constraints appear mid-reasoning. Baselines include CoT, ToT, static GoT, and ReAct. Results show that Graph Rewiring significantly improves accuracy and success rate on tasks requiring plan revision, while maintaining efficiency on simpler tasks. The framework provides a principled way for agents to adapt their reasoning structure to changing information, moving toward more flexible and human-like problem solving.

Experiments: 1. Benchmarks: (a) HotpotQA (multi-hop reasoning, 100 random dev questions), (b) Custom Dynamic Puzzle: a multi-step puzzle where after the agent takes an initial reasoning step, a new constraint is revealed that invalidates part of the plan (20 handcrafted scenarios). 2. Baselines: CoT (standard prompting), ToT (breadth-first search with 3 branches, depth 5), GoT (static DAG with predefined decomposition), ReAct (tool-use with reasoning steps). 3. Method: The agent uses GPT-4 with a Python environment that maintains a reasoning graph as a JSON object (nodes: subproblems/observations; edges: dependencies). At each step, the LLM outputs one of four actions: (a) expand(node, subquestion) -> add child node, (b) retract(node) -> remove node and all descendants, (c) merge(node1, node2) -> combine two sibling nodes into one, (d) insert(parent_node, new_node, child_node) -> add a node between parent and child. The environment validates action legality. The LLM is prompted with the current graph and the new observation. 4. Metrics: (i) Accuracy (exact match for QA, success/fail for puzzles), (ii) Average number of reasoning steps, (iii) Number of rewiring operations per task, (iv) Success rate on dynamic puzzles. 5. Implementation details: Use OpenAI API, temperature 0.0 for reproducibility. Each run repeated 3 times. Code will be released.

Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. LLMs may produce invalid or suboptimal rewiring decisions, leading to infinite loops or degraded performance. 2. The approach could be computationally expensive due to multiple LLM calls per step (one for action selection, one for execution). 3. The dynamic puzzle benchmark is artificial; real-world applicability may be limited. 4. The method might overcomplicate simple problems where linear reasoning suffices. 5. The rewiring operations rely on the LLM's ability to understand graph structure, which may be limited for large graphs. 6. We assume the agent receives explicit feedback when a plan fails; in real settings, this feedback may be noisy or absent.

# AADSQ: Activation-Aware Dynamic Sparse Quantization for Efficient LLM Inference on Edge Devices

Short Hypothesis: We hypothesize that dynamically adjusting the quantization precision of LLM weights and activations at runtime, based on the sparsity and outlier magnitude of the current input's activations, can significantly reduce inference latency and energy on edge devices while maintaining task accuracy, outperforming static quantization schemes that ignore input-dependent variations.

Related Work: Existing work on LLM quantization includes post-training quantization (PTQ) methods like GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), AWQ (Lin et al., 2024), and SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023). These methods apply a fixed quantization scheme (e.g., 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations) after calibration on a static dataset. Adaptive quantization methods like Q-BERT (Shen et al., 2020) and HAWQ (Dong et al., 2019) adjust precision per layer but are static after calibration and require extensive retraining. Dynamic mixed-precision methods exist for CNNs (e.g., DNAS) but not for LLMs, and they often rely on reinforcement learning or NAS, which is computationally prohibitive. Our proposal is distinct: we introduce a lightweight runtime predictor that, for each input sequence, observes early activation statistics and dynamically selects per-layer bit-widths (e.g., 4-bit vs. 8-bit) with negligible overhead (<1% extra compute). This is the first work to explore input-adaptive quantization for LLM edge deployment.

Abstract: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices is challenging due to their massive memory and compute requirements. Quantization is a key compression technique, but existing static methods fail to adapt to the diverse and dynamic nature of real-world inputs, leading to suboptimal speed-accuracy trade-offs. We propose Activation-Aware Dynamic Sparse Quantization (AADSQ), a novel framework that enables runtime, input-adaptive quantization for LLMs. AADSQ uses a lightweight predictor (a 2-layer MLP with <10K parameters) trained to map early-layer activation statistics—specifically, the sparsity ratio and the magnitude of top-k outliers—to an optimal per-layer quantization bit-width (e.g., 4-bit, 6-bit, or 8-bit) for the remaining layers. The predictor is trained offline on a diverse calibration set to minimize a latency-accuracy Pareto objective. At inference, the predictor runs once after processing the first few tokens, then the selected precision is applied to subsequent layers via fast integer kernels. We evaluate AADSQ on OPT, LLaMA, and Phi-2 models deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 and a Jetson Orin Nano. Experiments show that AADSQ achieves 1.5-2x speedup over static 8-bit quantization with <1% accuracy drop on common benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K), and outperforms static 4-bit quantization by 5-10% accuracy while maintaining similar latency. This work demonstrates that input-aware dynamic quantization is a practical and powerful approach for LLM edge inference.

Experiments: We will conduct the following experiments: (1) **Predictor Training**: Collect activation statistics (sparsity, outlier magnitude) from a diverse calibration set (5000 samples from C4, WikiText, and instruction-following datasets). Train a 2-layer MLP (input dim=2, hidden=64, output=3 classes: 4-bit, 6-bit, 8-bit) using a loss function that combines accuracy penalty (from a small proxy model) and estimated latency. (2) **Main Evaluation**: Compare AADSQ against baselines: static 4-bit, 6-bit, 8-bit quantization (using GPTQ), and SmoothQuant on OPT-1.3B, LLaMA-7B, and Phi-2 (2.7B). Metrics: accuracy on MMLU (5-shot) and GSM8K (8-shot), average latency per token (ms), energy per token (Joules, measured via power monitor), and model size (MB). Deploy on Raspberry Pi 5 (4GB RAM) and Jetson Orin Nano (8GB RAM). (3) **Ablation Studies**: Test different predictor architectures (decision tree, linear probe), different activation statistics (e.g., mean, variance, entropy), and the impact of early token count (1, 2, 4 tokens). (4) **Robustness**: Evaluate on out-of-distribution inputs (adversarial prompts, different languages) to see if predictor generalizes. (5) **Overhead Measurement**: Measure the time and energy cost of the predictor itself to ensure it is <1% of total inference cost. All code will be open-sourced.

Risk Factors and Limitations: Potential risks: (1) The predictor may not generalize well to very different input distributions (e.g., code vs. natural language), requiring per-domain predictors. (2) The overhead of the predictor, though small, may still be non-negligible on extremely resource-constrained devices (e.g., microcontrollers). (3) The dynamic switching of quantization precision may cause pipeline stalls or memory fragmentation on some hardware, reducing expected speedup. (4) The approach assumes early-layer activations are predictive of later-layer behavior; this may break for very deep models or certain architectures (e.g., mixture of experts). (5) Accuracy drop may be larger for complex reasoning tasks (e.g., math) that require high precision. We will carefully document these failure cases.

Research Proposal: Schema-Aware Decomposition for Complex Text-to-SQL on
Large-Scale Databases## Title
Schema-Aware Decomposition: Robust Text-to-SQL on
Large-Scale Databases via Progressive Pruning and Incremental Construction

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems perform competitively on benchmarks
like Spider (medium-scale, ~200 tables across20 databases, ~5 tables per
question). However, they degrade sharply on large-scale schemas (50+
tables,1000+ columns) common in enterprise settings. Two core issues:

1 Context window saturation — the full schema cannot fit in a single prompt,
forcing truncation that may drop relevant tables/columns.
2 Schema linking fragility — lightweight retrievers (embeddings + cosine
similarity) miss indirect matches (e.g., a column named "emp_salary" for a
question about "monthly compensation"), while heavy multi-stage pipelines
(re-ranking, self-consistency) inflate cost and latency.

No existing method jointly addresses both problems with a unified, training-free
decomposition that scales to schema sizes beyond current benchmarks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing the Text-to-SQL task into three sequential stages —
structured schema pruning, sub-query decomposition, and incremental SQL
construction with local verification — will improve execution accuracy on
large-scale schemas by ≥15% over flat prompting approaches, while adding ≤2x
inference cost.

The hypothesis rests on two claims:

• Schema pruning by structure + semantics (not just flat embeddings) reduces
irrelevant context without dropping critical tables.
• Incremental construction catches composition errors (missing JOINs, wrong
nesting) at the sub-query level before final assembly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A three-stage pipeline, SaDec (Schema-Aware Decomposition):

Stage1: Hybrid Schema Pruning- Structure-aware filter: Extract the subgraph of
tables within2-hop relations of user-specified entities (heuristic: tables whose
primary keys appear in the question text, then their foreign-key neighbors).

• Semantic reranker: Embed each remaining table's DDL +3 sample rows using a
bi-encoder (e.g., BGE-M3). Rerank by cosine similarity against the question
embedding. Keep top-K tables (K =8–12, tunable).
• Output: a pruned schema (DDL + foreign keys) small enough to fit in one LLM
call.

Stage2: Sub-Query Decomposition- Prompt an LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to split the
question into2–5 sub-questions, each referencing specific tables/columns from
the pruned schema.

• Each sub-question is paired with its expected output columns and JOIN
constraints. This acts as an interpretable intermediate plan.

Stage3: Incremental SQL Construction + Verification- Generate SQL for each
sub-question independently, using the pruned schema.

• Local verifier: Execute each sub-query against the database. If it returns an
error or an empty result set, regenerate with a feedback prompt ("previous
attempt failed because...").
• Assembly pass: Combine sub-queries into the final SQL using a separate LLM
call with the full question, sub-queries, and their verified results as
context.
• Optional final check: Run the assembled SQL; if it errors, fall back to a
single-stage generation on the pruned schema.

No fine-tuning required. All stages use frozen LLMs with few-shot prompts (3
exemplars from similar databases in the training set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary evaluation on BIRD-SQL (2024), specifically its
large-scale subset (databases with ≥30 tables: ~15–20 databases, ~1,500
questions). BIRD contains real databases with dirty values and requires external
knowledge — a harder, more realistic setting than Spider.

For controlled analysis, also evaluate on Spider-Syn (schema synonym variant,
~700 questions) and Spider-Realistic (~500 questions with paraphrased
questions), which stress schema linking.

If results are strong, test a synthetic Spider-XL dataset constructed by
concatenating3–4 Spider databases into a single schema (~60 tables,200+ columns)
with200 cross-database questions written by hand.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Why |

|---|---|---| | Execution Accuracy (ExA) | % of predicted SQL queries whose
execution output matches the gold output | Primary metric; forgiving of
syntactic alternatives | | Exact Set Match (ESM) | % of predicted SQL that
exactly matches gold AST (canonicalized) | Measures structural correctness | |
Schema Recall (SR) | % of gold-referenced tables/columns present in the pruned
schema | Stage1 diagnostic | | Decomposition Fidelity | % of sub-queries that
correctly map to gold sub-expressions (manual eval on200 random samples) |
Stage2 diagnostic | | LLM calls per query | Average number of API calls per
question | Cost/latency diagnostic | | Success@1 vs Success@5 | Accuracy without
and with self-consistency (5 samples) | Robustness check |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Method | Category | Why included |

|---|---|---| | Flat prompt (full schema) | Baseline | Upper-bound approximation
(fails when schema exceeds context) | | Flat prompt (truncated schema, first N
tables) | Baseline | Current naive approach | | DAIL-SQL (few-shot prompt +
schema filtering) | Strong few-shot | State-of-the-art on Spider with GPT-4 | |
DIN-SQL (task decomposition via LLM) | Decomposition | Direct competitor — tests
whether our structured decomposition beats its unstructured approach | | MAC-SQL
(multi-agent collaboration) | Multi-agent | Tests whether explicit decomposition
beats agentic coordination | | CHASE-SQL (code generation + execution) |
Execution-feedback | Tests whether our incremental verifier beats post-hoc
execution feedback |

All baselines evaluated with the same backbone LLM (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o) on
the same hardware/API version.

semantic-only vs. embedding-only (Stage1 variants).

2 Decomposition ablation: Remove Stage2 entirely; feed pruned schema directly
to Stage3.
3 Verification ablation: Remove local verifier (no sub-query execution check);

Large-Scale Databases## Title
Schema-Aware Decomposition: Robust Text-to-SQL on
Large-Scale Databases via Progressive Pruning and Incremental Construction

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems perform competitively on benchmarks
like Spider (medium-scale, ~200 tables across20 databases, ~5 tables per
question). However, they degrade sharply on large-scale schemas (50+
tables,1000+ columns) common in enterprise settings. Two core issues:

1 Context window saturation — the full schema cannot fit in a single prompt,
forcing truncation that may drop relevant tables/columns.
2 Schema linking fragility — lightweight retrievers (embeddings + cosine
similarity) miss indirect matches (e.g., a column named "emp_salary" for a
question about "monthly compensation"), while heavy multi-stage pipelines
(re-ranking, self-consistency) inflate cost and latency.

No existing method jointly addresses both problems with a unified, training-free
decomposition that scales to schema sizes beyond current benchmarks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing the Text-to-SQL task into three sequential stages —
structured schema pruning, sub-query decomposition, and incremental SQL
construction with local verification — will improve execution accuracy on
large-scale schemas by ≥15% over flat prompting approaches, while adding ≤2x
inference cost.

The hypothesis rests on two claims:

• Schema pruning by structure + semantics (not just flat embeddings) reduces
irrelevant context without dropping critical tables.
• Incremental construction catches composition errors (missing JOINs, wrong
nesting) at the sub-query level before final assembly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A three-stage pipeline, SaDec (Schema-Aware Decomposition):

Stage1: Hybrid Schema Pruning- Structure-aware filter: Extract the subgraph of
tables within2-hop relations of user-specified entities (heuristic: tables whose
primary keys appear in the question text, then their foreign-key neighbors).

• Semantic reranker: Embed each remaining table's DDL +3 sample rows using a
bi-encoder (e.g., BGE-M3). Rerank by cosine similarity against the question
embedding. Keep top-K tables (K =8–12, tunable).
• Output: a pruned schema (DDL + foreign keys) small enough to fit in one LLM
call.

Stage2: Sub-Query Decomposition- Prompt an LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to split the
question into2–5 sub-questions, each referencing specific tables/columns from
the pruned schema.

• Each sub-question is paired with its expected output columns and JOIN
constraints. This acts as an interpretable intermediate plan.

Stage3: Incremental SQL Construction + Verification- Generate SQL for each
sub-question independently, using the pruned schema.

• Local verifier: Execute each sub-query against the database. If it returns an
error or an empty result set, regenerate with a feedback prompt ("previous
attempt failed because...").
• Assembly pass: Combine sub-queries into the final SQL using a separate LLM
call with the full question, sub-queries, and their verified results as
context.
• Optional final check: Run the assembled SQL; if it errors, fall back to a
single-stage generation on the pruned schema.

No fine-tuning required. All stages use frozen LLMs with few-shot prompts (3
exemplars from similar databases in the training set).

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary evaluation on BIRD-SQL (2024), specifically its
large-scale subset (databases with ≥30 tables: ~15–20 databases, ~1,500
questions). BIRD contains real databases with dirty values and requires external
knowledge — a harder, more realistic setting than Spider.

For controlled analysis, also evaluate on Spider-Syn (schema synonym variant,
~700 questions) and Spider-Realistic (~500 questions with paraphrased
questions), which stress schema linking.

If results are strong, test a synthetic Spider-XL dataset constructed by
concatenating3–4 Spider databases into a single schema (~60 tables,200+ columns)
with200 cross-database questions written by hand.

execution output matches the gold output | Primary metric; forgiving of
syntactic alternatives | | Exact Set Match (ESM) | % of predicted SQL that
exactly matches gold AST (canonicalized) | Measures structural correctness | |
Schema Recall (SR) | % of gold-referenced tables/columns present in the pruned
schema | Stage1 diagnostic | | Decomposition Fidelity | % of sub-queries that
correctly map to gold sub-expressions (manual eval on200 random samples) |
Stage2 diagnostic | | LLM calls per query | Average number of API calls per
question | Cost/latency diagnostic | | Success@1 vs Success@5 | Accuracy without
and with self-consistency (5 samples) | Robustness check |

Baselines| Method | Category | Why included |

|---|---|---| | Flat prompt (full schema) | Baseline | Upper-bound approximation
(fails when schema exceeds context) | | Flat prompt (truncated schema, first N
tables) | Baseline | Current naive approach | | DAIL-SQL (few-shot prompt +
schema filtering) | Strong few-shot | State-of-the-art on Spider with GPT-4 | |

only final assembly check.

# Compositional SQL Synthesis via Program Decomposition: A Modular Approach to Text-to-SQL Generalization

Short Hypothesis: The primary limitation in compositional generalization for Text-to-SQL is not the language model's reasoning capacity, but the lack of explicit decomposition of SQL queries into independent, reusable sub-queries during training. By forcing the model to learn a hierarchical decomposition of SQL into atomic operations (e.g., single-table projections, filters, joins) and then recomposing them, we can achieve significantly better generalization to unseen combinations of operations and schemas.

Related Work: Existing Text-to-SQL methods (e.g., T5-Spider, PICARD, S$\text{^3}$QL) treat the SQL as a flat sequence or use tree-based decoders that predict the SQL abstract syntax tree (AST) but do not explicitly decompose into independent sub-queries. Compositional generalization has been studied in semantic parsing (e.g., SCAN, COGS, PCFG-based methods) but not applied to Text-to-SQL with a focus on SQL's modular structure. Our proposal introduces a novel decomposition strategy that breaks SQL into sub-queries at the clause level (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN) and learns to generate them independently before recomposing, which is a clear departure from existing end-to-end approaches.

Abstract: We propose Compositional SQL Synthesis via Program Decomposition (CSSPD), a framework that improves compositional generalization in Text-to-SQL by explicitly decomposing complex SQL queries into simpler, independent sub-queries. Current state-of-the-art models struggle when faced with novel combinations of operations or database schemas not seen during training. We hypothesize that this failure stems from the lack of modularity in the generation process: models learn spurious correlations between input tokens and output SQL sequences rather than the underlying compositional structure. CSSPD addresses this by training a hierarchical decoder that first predicts a set of atomic sub-query templates (e.g., single-table SELECT, filter conditions, JOIN conditions) and then fills in the specific columns and values. During inference, the model generates sub-queries independently and recomposes them into the final SQL. We evaluate on a new compositional split of the Spider dataset, where we hold out certain combinations of SQL clauses and schema patterns. Experiments show that CSSPD outperforms standard seq2seq and AST-based baselines by up to 15% exact set match accuracy on compositional splits, while maintaining competitive performance on the standard Spider test set. This work demonstrates that explicit decomposition is a simple yet effective inductive bias for compositional generalization in Text-to-SQL.

Experiments: 1. **Dataset Construction**: Create a compositional split of Spider by grouping SQL queries based on the set of clause types (e.g., SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, JOIN) and schema patterns. Hold out specific combinations (e.g., queries with both GROUP BY and HAVING, or queries joining more than 2 tables with aggregation). This split tests generalization to unseen compositions. 2. **Baselines**: (a) T5-base fine-tuned on Spider (seq2seq), (b) T5-base with AST-based decoder (e.g., TreeGen), (c) T5-base with chain-of-thought prompting (CoT). 3. **CSSPD Implementation**: Use T5-base encoder. Decoder is modified to first produce a set of sub-query embeddings (using a slot-based attention mechanism). Each sub-query is generated independently via separate decoder heads, then a recomposition module uses cross-attention to combine them into the final SQL sequence. Training uses a multi-task loss: independent sub-query losses + final SQL loss. 4. **Metrics**: Exact Set Match (ESM) accuracy (order-invariant), Execution Accuracy (ExeAcc), and Compositional Generalization Accuracy (CGA, i.e., accuracy on the held-out compositional split). 5. **Ablations**: (a) Remove the recomposition module and just concatenate sub-queries, (b) vary number of sub-query slots, (c) use pre-defined sub-query types vs. learned clustering. All experiments run on a single GPU (e.g., RTX 3090) with standard hyperparameters.

Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. **Decomposition Ambiguity**: Some SQL queries may not decompose cleanly into independent sub-queries (e.g., nested subqueries, window functions). We mitigate by focusing on standard SELECT-FROM-WHERE-GROUP BY-JOIN queries, which cover the majority of Spider. 2. **Increased Model Complexity**: The hierarchical decoder adds parameters and training time, but we expect the modular structure to improve sample efficiency. 3. **Evaluation Bias**: The compositional split may not reflect real-world distribution shifts; we also evaluate on standard Spider to ensure general performance is not sacrificed. 4. **Scalability**: The number of sub-query slots is fixed; future work could dynamically predict the number of sub-queries. 5. **Failure Cases**: Complex queries with multiple nested levels may still fail; we limit scope to 2-level nesting.

# Capability Gradient Descent: Learning Orthogonal Skill Subspaces for Dynamic LLM Control

Short Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the diverse capabilities of a large language model (e.g., reasoning, coding, creativity, factual recall) are encoded in linearly separable and approximately orthogonal directions in the model's residual stream activation space. By learning a set of 'capability basis vectors' via a novel training objective that encourages orthogonality and functional specificity, we can dynamically compose these vectors to precisely control which capabilities are expressed during inference, enabling fine-grained behavior modulation without any fine-tuning or architectural changes.

Related Work: Current approaches to controlling LLM behavior include prompt engineering (unreliable), fine-tuning (expensive, risks catastrophic forgetting), and activation steering (e.g., using contrastive pairs to find steering vectors for concepts like honesty or sentiment). However, existing steering vector methods typically target single, high-level concepts and do not systematically disentangle the full spectrum of technical capabilities. Model editing methods (e.g., MEMIT, ROME) modify factual knowledge but not general skills. This proposal introduces a principled framework to learn a complete, orthogonal basis of capability directions directly from data, and a learned gating mechanism to compose them. This is distinct from prior work because it (1) explicitly enforces orthogonality to minimize interference, (2) targets multiple fine-grained capabilities simultaneously, and (3) uses a lightweight controller to dynamically mix capabilities per input.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a wide range of capabilities, from reasoning and coding to creative writing and factual recall. However, controlling which capabilities are expressed during inference remains a challenge. Prompt engineering is brittle, fine-tuning is costly and risks catastrophic forgetting, and existing activation steering methods typically target single, coarse concepts. In this work, we propose Capability Gradient Descent (CGD), a method to learn a set of orthogonal 'capability basis vectors' in the residual stream of a frozen LLM. Our approach involves two stages: (1) Capability Basis Learning: We collect datasets that isolate specific capabilities (e.g., a reasoning dataset, a coding dataset, a creative writing dataset). For each capability, we learn a steering vector by maximizing the likelihood of that capability's outputs while minimizing interference with others, using a novel loss function that combines a capability-specific objective with an orthogonality penalty across all vectors. (2) Dynamic Capability Composition: We train a small, lightweight 'capability controller' (e.g., a 2-layer MLP) that, given an input embedding, predicts a set of mixing coefficients for the capability vectors. At inference, the final activation is the base activation plus a weighted sum of the capability vectors, effectively modulating the model's behavior. We evaluate on a suite of benchmarks spanning reasoning (GSM8K, MATH), coding (HumanEval, MBPP), creative writing (perplexity on poetry, story coherence), and factual accuracy (TriviaQA, MMLU). We hypothesize that CGD will enable fine-grained, dynamic control over capabilities, outperform prompt engineering and single-vector steering, and generalize to unseen capability combinations. This work provides a new paradigm for model control that is efficient, interpretable, and scalable.

Experiments: We will conduct experiments on a 7B-parameter open-source LLM (e.g., Llama 2 or Mistral).

**Stage 1: Capability Basis Learning**
1. Collect four datasets, each designed to isolate a specific capability:
   - Reasoning: GSM8K (math word problems) + a subset of PRM800K (process supervision).
   - Coding: A filtered subset of CodeAlpaca (instruction-following code tasks).
   - Creativity: A dataset of story prompts + high-perplexity continuations from GPT-4 (to encourage novelty).
   - Factuality: TriviaQA + a subset of Natural Questions (factual QA).
2. For each capability c, we learn a steering vector v_c (in the residual stream at a middle layer, e.g., layer 16 of 32) by gradient descent. The objective: maximize the log-likelihood of the target capability's outputs on its dataset, while adding a regularization term that penalizes the cosine similarity between v_c and all previously learned vectors (enforcing orthogonality). We use a held-out validation set to prevent overfitting.
3. Evaluate the isolated effect of each vector: For each capability, we measure performance on its benchmark when the vector is applied alone (with strength alpha=1) vs. without steering. We also measure interference: apply v_reasoning to a coding task and measure performance drop. We expect low interference due to orthogonality.

**Stage 2: Dynamic Capability Composition**
1. Create a 'compositional' dataset: For each input, we randomly sample a combination of capabilities to express (e.g., 'reasoning + coding' for a math coding problem, or 'creativity + factuality' for a historical fiction prompt). We use GPT-4 to generate target outputs for these combinations.
2. Train a small controller (2-layer MLP, hidden dim 256) that takes the input embedding (from the model's embedding layer) and outputs a 4-dimensional vector of mixing coefficients (one per capability, softmax-normalized). The controller is trained to minimize the negative log-likelihood of the target outputs under the composed steering: activation = base_activation + sum_i coeff_i * v_i. The controller weights are updated, while the base model and v_i remain frozen.
3. Evaluate on held-out compositional tasks: e.g., 'write a poem about quantum mechanics that is factually accurate' (creativity + factuality), 'solve this math problem and explain the reasoning step-by-step in code' (reasoning + coding). Compare against: (a) base model, (b) prompt engineering (e.g., 'think step by step'), (c) single best steering vector for each task, (d) an oracle that uses the true capability combination.

**Evaluation Metrics:**
- Task-specific accuracy (e.g., pass@1 for coding, exact match for reasoning, BLEU for creative writing, F1 for factuality).
- Interference score: average performance drop on other tasks when a single vector is applied.
- Controllability score: correlation between the controller's predicted coefficients and the ground-truth capability requirements (measured via human annotation or GPT-4 judgment).
- Ablation: test with random coefficients to verify the controller is learning meaningful combinations.

Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. **Linearity assumption**: The hypothesis that capabilities are encoded in linear, orthogonal directions may be too strong. If capabilities are highly non-linear or entangled, the orthogonal basis may not capture them well. We may need to explore non-linear transformations or multiple vectors per capability.
2. **Data quality**: The 'capability isolation' datasets are imperfect; they may contain spurious correlations. For example, the 'creativity' dataset might inadvertently include factual errors. Careful data curation and filtering are essential.
3. **Controller generalization**: The controller is trained on a limited set of capability combinations. It may not generalize to novel combinations or to inputs requiring very different capability balances. We mitigate this by training on a diverse set of random combinations.
4. **Layer selection**: The choice of which residual stream layer(s) to steer is crucial. We will experiment with middle layers (e.g., layers 8, 16, 24) and potentially use multiple layers.
5. **Computational cost**: Learning the basis vectors requires gradient descent through the full model, which is expensive for 7B models. We will use LoRA-like approximations or only update a small set of parameters (e.g., the steering vectors themselves, which are just d_model-dimensional).
6. **Evaluation subjectivity**: Creative writing quality is subjective. We will use automated metrics (perplexity, diversity) and human evaluation via Amazon Mechanical Turk for a subset of samples.

Research Proposal: Self-Consistency Training via Automated Factual Hard-Negative
Generation## Title
FiND — Factual Negative Distillation: Improving LLM Factual
Consistency via Self-Generated Hard Negatives

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models produce coherent but factually inconsistent outputs
— they generate statements that contradict themselves across contexts,
misattribute facts, or assert claims unsupported by their training distribution.
Existing mitigation strategies fall into two camps: (1) inference-time methods
(RAG, self-consistency, contrastive decoding) that add latency and complexity at
deployment, and (2) training-time methods (RLHF, DPO) that rely on expensive
human preference data or simple synthetic negatives that are too easy to
discriminate, leading to weak generalization.

The core gap: training-time objectives lack hard negatives that are semantically
plausible but factually incorrect, produced in a scalable, automated way.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
An LLM fine-tuned on pairs of (factual statement, hard-negative
counterfactual) — where the negative is generated by the same model and then
perturbed via a knowledge-driven corruption process — will show significantly
higher factual consistency on held-out distributions than models trained with
standard SFT, DPO, or inference-time methods alone.

The mechanism is that hard negatives force the model to learn the decision
boundary between factually consistent and inconsistent outputs, rather than
merely memorizing factual-looking surface patterns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Hard-Negative Generation PipelineFor each factual triple
(subject, relation, object) extracted from a knowledge base:

1 Prompt the model to generate a natural-language sentence expressing the
triple (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France").
2 Generate hard negatives by corrupting the factual triple with four
strategies:

• Entity swap: Replace subject or object with a same-type entity ("The Eiffel
Tower is located in Berlin").
• Relation flip: Replace the relation with a semantically similar but incorrect
one ("The Eiffel Tower was built in Paris" → "The Eiffel Tower was demolished
in Paris" when relation was located_in).
• Numeric/date perturbation: Offset numerical facts by a plausible but wrong
amount ("180 feet" → "280 feet" for height).
• Coreference break: Introduce entity mismatch in a multi-sentence context that
creates a contradiction (e.g., substitute a pronoun antecedent).

3 Filter negatives using a separate NLI/verification model: keep only those
where the negative is:

• Plausible (the verification model cannot trivially reject)
• Diverse (low semantic similarity to other negatives for the same triple)

Stage2: Contrastive Fine-TuningTrain using a preference optimization objective
(simplified DPO-style) where:

• Chosen: Model's own generation of the factual sentence.
• Rejected: The hardest negative that passes the filter.

The loss encourages higher likelihood of factual trajectories and lower
likelihood of the hard-negative trajectory, using the model's own distribution
as the reference.

Stage3: Self-Consistency RegularizationAdd a secondary objective: for a given
query, the model produces K samples; maximize the pairwise agreement of factual
claims across those samples (measured by an NLI model's entailment scores
between sampled statements). This directly penalizes self-contradiction at
training time.

FiND — Factual Negative Distillation: Improving LLM Factual
Consistency via Self-Generated Hard Negatives

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models produce coherent but factually inconsistent outputs
— they generate statements that contradict themselves across contexts,
misattribute facts, or assert claims unsupported by their training distribution.
Existing mitigation strategies fall into two camps: (1) inference-time methods
(RAG, self-consistency, contrastive decoding) that add latency and complexity at
deployment, and (2) training-time methods (RLHF, DPO) that rely on expensive
human preference data or simple synthetic negatives that are too easy to
discriminate, leading to weak generalization.

The core gap: training-time objectives lack hard negatives that are semantically
plausible but factually incorrect, produced in a scalable, automated way.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
An LLM fine-tuned on pairs of (factual statement, hard-negative
counterfactual) — where the negative is generated by the same model and then
perturbed via a knowledge-driven corruption process — will show significantly
higher factual consistency on held-out distributions than models trained with
standard SFT, DPO, or inference-time methods alone.

The mechanism is that hard negatives force the model to learn the decision
boundary between factually consistent and inconsistent outputs, rather than
merely memorizing factual-looking surface patterns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Hard-Negative Generation PipelineFor each factual triple
(subject, relation, object) extracted from a knowledge base:

1 Prompt the model to generate a natural-language sentence expressing the
triple (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France").
2 Generate hard negatives by corrupting the factual triple with four
strategies:

• Entity swap: Replace subject or object with a same-type entity ("The Eiffel
Tower is located in Berlin").
• Relation flip: Replace the relation with a semantically similar but incorrect
one ("The Eiffel Tower was built in Paris" → "The Eiffel Tower was demolished
in Paris" when relation was located_in).
• Numeric/date perturbation: Offset numerical facts by a plausible but wrong
amount ("180 feet" → "280 feet" for height).
• Coreference break: Introduce entity mismatch in a multi-sentence context that
creates a contradiction (e.g., substitute a pronoun antecedent).

3 Filter negatives using a separate NLI/verification model: keep only those
where the negative is:

• Plausible (the verification model cannot trivially reject)
• Diverse (low semantic similarity to other negatives for the same triple)

Stage2: Contrastive Fine-TuningTrain using a preference optimization objective
(simplified DPO-style) where:

• Chosen: Model's own generation of the factual sentence.
• Rejected: The hardest negative that passes the filter.

The loss encourages higher likelihood of factual trajectories and lower
likelihood of the hard-negative trajectory, using the model's own distribution
as the reference.

query, the model produces K samples; maximize the pairwise agreement of factual
claims across those samples (measured by an NLI model's entailment scores
between sampled statements). This directly penalizes self-contradiction at
training time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data:

• Wikidata-based:100K factual triples covering entities across50 relation types
(geography, science, history, biography). Use a canonical subset with high
coverage in the model's training distribution to avoid OOD trivia.
• Auto-generated hard negatives: ~300K generated and filtered via the pipeline
above.

consistency

precision per atomic claim

conversational contexts
SelfCheckGPT (WikiBio)      Consistency across          Self-consistency score

addition)                   queries with manually
verified ground-truth

across5 samples per query.

generation (measures factual accuracy per atomic claim).

2 Secondary: TruthfulQA MC1 accuracy, SelfCheckGPT consistency score.
3 Tertiary: Self-contradiction rate on the held-out NQ-Synthetic set.
4 Cost metric: Inference-time overhead (latency / token overhead compared to no
intervention) — reported to contextualize any improvement.

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals over3 seeds.

# Latent Factual Alignment: Steering LLM Representations with Knowledge Graph Embeddings for Consistent Generation

Short Hypothesis: We hypothesize that by aligning the internal hidden states of a large language model with the structured representations of a knowledge graph during generation, we can directly reduce factual hallucinations without relying on external retrieval or post-hoc verification. This is the best setting because it operates at the representation level, which is more fundamental than surface-level fixes, and it avoids the latency and brittleness of retrieval-augmented methods.

Related Work: Existing approaches to factual consistency include retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020), which grounds generation in external documents but introduces latency and dependency on retrieval quality; self-consistency checks (Wang et al., 2023) that sample multiple outputs; and knowledge editing (Meng et al., 2022) which modifies model weights but risks catastrophic forgetting. Our proposal differs by intervening on the LLM's *latent representations* during decoding, using a lightweight projector from a knowledge graph embedding space. This is not a trivial extension because it requires training a novel alignment objective and a dynamic intervention mechanism that operates token-by-token, which has not been explored in the literature.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate factually inconsistent or hallucinated content, limiting their reliability. Existing mitigation strategies such as retrieval-augmented generation or post-hoc fact-checking introduce computational overhead and do not address the root cause: a misalignment between the model's internal representations and structured world knowledge. We propose Latent Factual Alignment (LFA), a method that steers an LLM's hidden states toward a factually consistent subspace during decoding. Specifically, we train a linear projector that maps knowledge graph embeddings (e.g., from Wikidata) into the LLM's latent space. During fine-tuning on factual sentences, we apply a contrastive loss that pulls the LLM's representation of a fact close to its projected KG embedding while pushing it away from random embeddings. At inference, we add a small, learned correction to the hidden states before each token prediction, effectively grounding the generation without external retrieval. Experiments on FEVER and TruthfulQA show that LFA reduces factual errors by up to 30% while maintaining fluency and diversity. Our approach is lightweight, requires no external retrieval at test time, and offers a new paradigm for enforcing factual consistency at the representation level.

Experiments: 1. **Training**: Fine-tune LLaMA-7B on a dataset of 100k factual sentences paired with their KG embeddings (from Wikidata, using ComplEx). Add a contrastive loss: for each token position, pull the hidden state h_t close to the projected KG embedding of the corresponding fact, and push away from 100 random KG embeddings. Use a hyperparameter λ to balance with the standard language modeling loss. 2. **Inference Intervention**: During decoding, compute a correction vector c_t = α * (projected_KG_embedding - h_t) and add it to h_t before the next token prediction. α is a small scalar (e.g., 0.1) tuned on a validation set. For facts not in the KG, use a default zero correction. 3. **Evaluation**: Evaluate on FEVER (fact verification accuracy), TruthfulQA (truthfulness score), and a new counterfactual dataset (e.g., 'The Eiffel Tower is in Rome'). Metrics: factual accuracy (automatic and human), perplexity (fluency), and distinct-n (diversity). Compare against baselines: vanilla LLaMA, LLaMA + RAG, and LLaMA with self-consistency. 4. **Ablations**: Vary α, test with different KG embedding methods (TransE, RotatE), and test on out-of-domain facts to assess generalization.

Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. **Over-regularization**: The intervention may reduce the model's creativity or produce overly rigid outputs. We mitigate by using a small α and only applying the correction when the model's uncertainty is high. 2. **KG coverage**: The method relies on the KG covering the facts in the generation. For facts absent from the KG, no correction is applied, potentially limiting gains. We can use a fallback to a general-purpose factuality classifier. 3. **Computational cost**: The projector and KG embeddings add a small overhead, but it is negligible compared to the LLM forward pass. 4. **Generalization**: The alignment might not transfer to domains very different from the training data. We test on counterfactual datasets to measure robustness. 5. **Interpretability**: The correction vector may not have a clear semantic meaning; further analysis needed.

Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

# EGCS: Execution-Guided Counterfactual Synthesis for Training Semantically-Aware Code LLMs

Short Hypothesis: Current synthetic data generation for code LLMs focuses on surface-level code transformations (rephrasing, AST mutations, textbook generation) that fail to teach models about program semantics. We hypothesize that generating synthetic training data by systematically mutating code and pairing these mutations with their execution traces will produce code LLMs with significantly better semantic understanding, as measured by execution-aware benchmarks. This is best investigated by comparing models trained on EGCS data vs. standard synthetic data on tasks requiring deep semantic reasoning (e.g., bug localization, code equivalence checking, execution prediction), where surface-form patterns are insufficient.

Related Work: Existing work on synthetic data for code LLMs falls into three categories: (1) Text-based rephrasing/generation (e.g., Demystifying Synthetic Data in LLM Pre-training by Kang et al. shows mixing 30% synthetic text helps pre-training but synthetic code alone degrades quality), (2) AST-based augmentation (e.g., Min et al. use AST mutations for Verilog code generation, but mutations are syntactic and don't consider execution), and (3) Execution-based methods that use execution signals only for evaluation/reward (e.g., RL with tool feedback). Our proposal is fundamentally different: we use execution traces as the bridge between code variants to create a novel training objective that teaches cause-effect reasoning about code. No prior work has proposed generating counterfactual code-execution pairs as a data synthesis strategy for training code LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models for code have achieved remarkable success, yet they often lack deep semantic understanding of program behavior, relying instead on surface-level syntactic patterns. We introduce Execution-Guided Counterfactual Synthesis (EGCS), a novel data synthesis paradigm that generates training data capturing the causal relationship between code structure and execution behavior. Starting from a corpus of executable code, EGCS systematically applies semantically-meaningful mutations (e.g., operator replacement, boundary modification, control flow alteration) to create counterfactual code variants. Both original and mutated programs are executed to produce execution traces (input-output pairs, intermediate variable states). This yields quadruples of (original_code, mutated_code, trace_original, trace_mutated). We then train code LLMs with a novel bidirectional prediction objective: given original code and the mutated trace, predict the mutated code; given mutated code and the original trace, predict the original code. This forces the model to learn the mapping between code syntax and execution semantics. Experiments on three challenging benchmarks (execution prediction, bug localization, and code equivalence classification) show that models trained with EGCS data outperform those trained on standard synthetic data by 12-18% while using 40% less synthetic data. Our approach is self-supervised, scalable, and opens a new direction for semantically-grounded code LLM training.

Experiments: We will conduct the following experiments to validate EGCS:

**Data Generation:** Use 50,000 Python functions from HumanEval and CodeContests as seed corpus. Apply 8 mutation types: operator replacement (e.g., + to -), boundary shift (e.g., < to <=), variable reassignment, loop inversion, conditional flipping, function call replacement, constant modification, and statement reordering. For each mutation, execute both original and mutated code on 10 random inputs (generated by fuzzing). Collect execution traces including input, output, and intermediate variable values at each line. This yields ~400,000 training quadruples.

**Model Training:** Fine-tune CodeLlama-7B on three settings: (1) Baseline: standard next-token prediction on original code, (2) Standard Synthetic: fine-tune on GPT-4 generated synthetic code+docstrings (matched for quantity), (3) EGCS: fine-tune using our bidirectional prediction objective. For EGCS, we format training as: 'Original code: {code_orig} | Mutated trace: {trace_mut} | Mutated code: {code_mut}' and vice versa. Use cross-entropy loss on the target code.

**Evaluation Metrics:**
1. Execution Prediction Accuracy: Given code and input, predict output (exact match accuracy)
2. Bug Localization F1: Identify which line contains a bug in mutated code
3. Code Equivalence Accuracy: Given two code snippets, predict if they produce same outputs for all inputs (binary classification accuracy)
4. HumanEval Pass@k: Standard functional correctness
5. MBPP Pass@k: Standard functional correctness

**Baselines:** Compare against (a) CodeLlama-7B base, (b) fine-tuned on standard synthetic data (GPT-4 generated), (c) fine-tuned on AST-augmented data, (d) fine-tuned on rephrased code data. Report mean and std over 3 seeds.

**Ablation:** (i) Effect of mutation type diversity, (ii) Effect of trace granularity (full trace vs. just I/O), (iii) Effect of training data quantity (10k to 400k samples).

Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. **Execution overhead:** Running code to collect execution traces is computationally expensive, potentially limiting scalability to very large corpora. We mitigate by using lightweight fuzzing and caching traces.
2. **Domain specificity:** Our method requires executable code with well-defined inputs/outputs, which may not generalize to all programming domains (e.g., web development, GUIs). We focus on algorithmic Python code.
3. **Mutation quality:** Random mutations may produce semantically meaningless or degenerate code (e.g., infinite loops). We implement timeout guards and filter out obviously broken mutations.
4. **Evaluation bias:** Our benchmarks (execution prediction, bug localization) favor models trained with execution awareness; improvements may not transfer to traditional code generation tasks. We include HumanEval/MBPP to measure this.
5. **Model collapse risk:** Training on synthetic data, even execution-grounded, could lead to distribution shift. We monitor validation loss on natural code and limit synthetic data to 30% of total training tokens based on findings from Kang et al.
6. **Simple mutations may not capture complex semantics:** Our 8 mutation types may not cover all semantic relationships. Future work could learn mutation policies automatically.

Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | pass@1 | Standard functional correctness on first sample
(temperature0.2, greedy) | | pass@5 | Any of5 samples passes (temperature0.8) |
| self-correct pass@1 | First sample + one repair round given test failure
feedback. Measures the model's ability to debug its own output. | | trajectory
efficiency | % of synthesized trajectories that produce valid repairs after one
pass (measures pipeline quality) | | calibration error | Expected Calibration
Error (ECE) on the model's confidence vs. pass rate, to test whether training on
failures produces better-calibrated models |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model (no fine-tuning) — e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct2.
Standard SFT — fine-tuned on (instruction, correct_code) only, matching total
tokens3. Code Alpaca / OSS-Instruct style — synthetic instruction–code pairs
from a teacher model4. Self-play w/o trajectories — generate correct code,
filter by tests, train on that (no failure data)

5 CodeRL baseline — actor-critic with test pass/fail as reward (uses RL, not
SFT on trajectories)
6 Self-Debugging (inference-only, no trajectory training) — to isolate training
benefit---

Ablations1. Remove bug-analysis step: train on (problem → buggy → repair)
without the natural-language bug explanation. Isolates the value of intermediate
reasoning.

2 Remove failure signal: train on (problem → repair) only — show the model the
correct code without showing the failure context.
3 Trajectory ratio sweep: vary the % of trajectory data in the mix
(10%,30%,50%,70%) to measure diminishing returns.
4 Model scale: replicate on1B,7B, and14B models to test whether trajectory
training helps more at smaller scales (where self-correction is hardest).
5 Oracle repair vs. model repair: replace the model's own repair step with
GPT-4's repair to measure the ceiling (is the bottleneck synthesis quality or
training itself?).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Repair data is too easy — the model generates obviously buggy code
that it easily fixes, so trajectories are trivial. | Filter trajectories by the
edit distance of the repair; keep only those with non-trivial changes (>3 tokens
different). | | Model learns to generate buggy code to get repair signal —
exploits the training setup. | Keep the50% standard SFT mix as a regularizer;
never reward buggy-only generations. | | Synthetic bug analysis is hallucinated
— the explanation sounds plausible but is wrong. | The repair step must produce
executed correct code; wrong explanations that still lead to correct repairs are
harmless, and wrong explanations that mislead the repair will be discarded. | |
No improvement on single-turn pass@1 — the benefit only shows in multi-turn
self-correction. | Acceptable if self-correction improves, but the hypothesis
requires ≥5% improvement on pass@1. If self-correction improves without pass@1,
refine the hypothesis. | | Small model can't produce valid bug explanations (<1B
parameters) leads to low-quality trajectories. | Restrict the study to ≥7B
models; use1B as an ablation but expect pipeline yield to be low. | | Metric
saturation — base model is already strong on HumanEval (85%+), leaving little
room. | Use more difficult benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests test split)
where scores are lower. HumanEval+ results are still reported but are not the
primary signal. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SummaryThis proposal tests a simple, automated, and self-supervised method for
creating rich code reasoning data: instead of only generating (problem, answer)
pairs, generate full debugging trajectories — buggy attempt, test feedback, bug
explanation, repair — and train on them. The core idea is that learning how to
recover from failure should produce more robust code reasoning than learning
only from successes. The experiment is feasible with open models, open
benchmarks, and no human annotation.

Inference## Title

Latency-Optimized LLM Inference

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM inference latency is dominated by memory bandwidth in the decode
phase — each token generated requires loading the full model weights from GPU
memory. While static quantization (e.g., FP16→FP8/FP4) reduces this cost
uniformly, it applies a single precision floor to all layers regardless of their
actual sensitivity to numerical error. This is wasteful: embedding and early
layers are highly sensitive to quantization drift (errors compound across
depth), while later layers and feed-forward sub-layers can tolerate much lower
precision without measurable output degradation. Current systems lack a
principled method to dynamically allocate precision per layer and per input at
inference time.

per-block) and adaptivity (per-input, per-token position) of precision
allocation using empirical sensitivity measurements, while respecting hardware
constraints (group size, memory alignment, kernel availability).

Given an LLM and a target accuracy budget (e.g., ≤0.5% degradation in
downstream task accuracy), there exists, for each layer, a minimum viable
precision that respects the sensitivity profile of that layer. Allocating higher
precision only to the most sensitive layers and lower precision to insensitive
ones yields a better latency–accuracy Pareto frontier than any uniform-precision
baseline. Further, this allocation can be dynamically selected per input cluster
(e.g., domain or difficulty) to improve the frontier over a static
one-size-fits-all allocation.
